The report provides an analysis of foreign affairs appropriations in the United States from 1996 to 2020. Prior to 2008, foreign affairs appropriations were spread across multiple bills, with funding often delayed or enacted late in the fiscal year. In 2008, appropriations for foreign operations were consolidated into one bill, the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations Act.

The report notes that since 1996, foreign affairs appropriations have primarily been enacted through omnibus or continuing resolution legislation, rather than standalone bills. In the past 25 years, there have only been three instances where foreign affairs appropriations were enacted on time and as standalone bills.

The report also highlights the use of emergency supplemental appropriations and Overseas Contingency Operations (OCO) funding. Prior to 2012, emergency supplemental appropriations were used to address unexpected budget needs, while OCO funding was used to fund military operations abroad. However, in 2012, the Obama Administration requested and Congress appropriated OCO funds for non-military foreign operations. Since then, OCO funding has ranged from 14% to 33% of total foreign affairs appropriations.

The report notes that the Budget Control Act of 2011 and subsequent Budget and Appropriations Acts have had a significant impact on foreign affairs funding. The BCA sets discretionary spending limits, but OCO funding is not counted against these limits, putting downward pressure on base funding for foreign operations. The 2015 and 2018 Budget and Appropriations Acts have had opposite effects on OCO funding for foreign operations, with the 2015 Act significantly increasing OCO funding and the 2018 Act allowing lawmakers to shift OCO funding back into base accounts.

The report concludes by noting that the use of emergency supplemental appropriations and OCO funding has become a common practice in recent years, and that the consolidation of foreign affairs appropriations into one bill has led to more predictable funding for some programs, but also increased pressure to use OCO funding for ongoing operations. The report suggests that reforms to the appropriations process could help ensure more stable and predictable funding for foreign operations.

answers: Congress currently appropriates most foreign affairs funding through annual Department of State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs (SFOPS) appropriations. Prior to FY2008, however, Congress provided funding for the Department of State, international broadcasting, and related programs within the Commerce, Justice, State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies appropriations. In those years, Congress separately appropriated funding for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and foreign aid within the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs appropriations. The 110th Congress aligned the two foreign affairs appropriations into the SFOPS legislation. SFOPS appropriations since FY2001 have included enduring appropriations (ongoing or base funding), emergency supplemental appropriations, and Overseas Contingency Operations (OCO) appropriations. Total SFOPS funding levels in both current and constant dollars show a general upward trend, with FY2004 as the peak largely as a result of emergency supplemental appropriations for Iraq Relief and Reconstruction Funds. When adjusted for inflation, annual foreign affairs appropriations have yet to surpass the FY2004 peak. The Budget Control Act (BCA) of 2011 and the Bipartisan Budget Acts (BBA) of 2015 and 2018 appear to have had an impact on both enduring and OCO funding levels. The legislative history of SFOPS appropriations shows that nearly all foreign affairs appropriations measures within the past 25 years were passed within omnibus, consolidated, or full-year continuing resolutions, rather than in stand-alone bills. Moreover, many appropriations were passed after the start of the new fiscal year, at times more than half way into the new fiscal year. In many fiscal years, SFOPS appropriations included emergency supplemental funding or, since FY2012, OCO funding.
